subject: Evidence tunnel: Splunk collector onboarding and TLS proxy options

From: Alice Chen <alice.chen@acme-security.com>

Cc: acme-sysadmin@acme.com

Subject: Evidence tunnel: Splunk collector onboarding and TLS proxy options

Hi Logan / Kimberly,

Thanks for taking this on — we need a lightweight, auditable way to get Redwoods' runtime logs (request traces + token-level telemetry for a small subset) into our Splunk instance for the SOC team. A couple constraints from our side:

- No direct outbound internet egress from the private subnet running the model pods (VPC-only).
- All connections must be mutually authenticated (mTLS) or use pre-provisioned client certs.
- We prefer push from a customer-side forwarder (so logs never originate on public IPs), but can accept a pull-collector if it sits behind our proxy.
- Retention and PII redaction: we will only accept structured events that strip full prompt text (we'll redact before ingest).

Attached is a sample Splunk HEC config we mocked up (splunk-collector-sample-config.yaml). High-level asks:

1) Can Redwood run a minimal forwarder inside a private subnet that connects to our Splunk HEC via a customer-managed proxy/bastion?
2) If not, list the options you support (HEC over mTLS, syslog over TCP TLS, S3-bucket pull via signed URL, Kafka tap).
3) Provide a short checklist of required network artifacts (IP ranges, ports, cert CNs) and an estimate of engineering effort.

Can we have a 30-minute sync this week to align on the approach?

Thanks,

Alice Chen
Senior Security Engineer, Acme Security
alice.chen@acme-security.com

From: logan.wright@redwood.com <logan.wright@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Evidence tunnel: Splunk collector onboarding and TLS proxy options

Alice — thanks for the clear constraints. I pulled together three pragmatic patterns we can offer; short summary and next steps below. I've attached a two-page options brief (redwood-evidence-tunnel-options.pdf) for internal reference.

Options (tradeoffs in one line):

1) Customer-side forwarder -> Splunk HEC (preferred)
   - Forwarder runs in your VPC (EC2/container), accepts log push from our private-forwarder via the customer-managed bastion or VPC peering.
   - Authentication: mTLS between our forwarder and your forwarder, mutual certs; Splunk accepts on private IP.
   - Pros: No public egress, minimal footprint on Redwood side.
   - Cons: Requires you to host a small VM/container and open internal port(s).

2) Forwarder-proxy in customer bastion (TLS passthrough)
   - We deploy a lightweight forwarder into a dedicated subnet that only talks to your bastion over an approved tunnel (SSH tunnel or IPsec).
   - Authentication: client certs + IP allowlist.
   - Pros: Simpler for customers without a forwarder; works with strict egress controls.
   - Cons: Network handoff complexity; requires bastion ops coordination.

3) Indirect ingestion via object store (S3-compatible) + pull
   - Redwood writes compressed batches to a customer-owned S3 bucket via a presigned URL. Your ingest pipeline pulls and forwards to Splunk.
   - Pros: Resilient, low blast radius, easy to vet artifacts.
   - Cons: Near-real-time only (batching), extra storage governance.

Network checklist (initial):
- Ports: 443 (HEC), optional 514/6514 (syslog TLS) if using syslog path.
- Certs: Fingerprint for Redwood client cert (we can generate CSR if needed); expected CNs: client.redwood-inference.com or customer-provided CNs.
- IPs: We prefer using customer allowlist for Redwood egress IPs when using forwarder-proxy; otherwise use the bastion tunnel.

Engineering estimate: 2-3 engineering days to validate handshake and sample ingestion for option (1) or (2) assuming certs and allowlist are provided; 4-6 days for option (3) including S3 lifecycle config and sample pipeline.

Proposed next step: 30-min sync to pick pattern + exchange certs/ips. I can run a short demo of the forwarder and show example unit events (redacted).

Best,

Logan Wright
Security Integrations Lead, Redwood Inference
logan.wright@redwood.com
--
Attachment: redwood-evidence-tunnel-options.pdf (application/pdf, 120 KB)

Looping in compliance and a quick note on guardrails.

- SOC 2 requirements: encryption in transit (TLS 1.2+), key rotation policy, and a documented data minimization step (we already support filters to strip full prompt text).
- For mTLS we will need the certificate chain and expected subject CNs; if Acme provides a CA we can trust that CA for the test.
- Please add required IP ranges and any proxy fingerprint to the checklist.

We should also confirm retention windows on the collection side; we can enforce redaction at source and generate an evidence bundle for audits when needed.

Kimberly Park
Head of Product Security, Redwood Inference
kimberly.park@redwood.com

Thanks — that all sounds reasonable. Quick answers to unblock you:

- We can host a tiny forwarder container in our private subnet (option 1 preferred). Ops will open 443 between the forwarder and the bastion; no public IP on the forwarder.
- We will provide a customer-managed CA and can generate client certs for mTLS. Expected CNs: acme-forwarder.acme.internal and acme-bastion.acme.internal.
- IP allowlist: we'll share a short-lived list (10.10.20.0/28) for the test window.
- Retention: 90 days on raw events, 7 days for pseudo-identifiers (per legal guidance).

Let's take the 30-min slot on Monday 10:00 AM PT to do the handshake and exchange certs. I'll bring our sysadmin (acme-sysadmin@acme.com) for network config.
